subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
You want to know why I'm running the anti-bullying stall at the fest? Okay.
I'm Seema, second year. Last semester in the canteen, a group from our class poured water over Tanvir's notes and called him "topper-bhai" while half the room filmed it. I was at the next table. I laughed once, nervously, and then just stared at my plate.
That night I couldn't sleep. I kept seeing his face, trying to smile. For a week I avoided him in the corridors, because I couldn't look at him.
Then it hit me: hiding was just doing nothing a second time. So I went up to him in the library and said, "I watched and did nothing. I'm sorry." He was quiet, then said, "Thanks for saying it. Most people pretend they weren't there."
So I've decided. Next time, I'm the one who says stop, or goes to a teacher. That's why I'm at this stall.

qa.q: What did the group pour over Tanvir's notes?
qa.a: They poured water over Tanvir's notes.

qa.q: How did Seema feel in the week after the canteen incident?
qa.a: Seema felt ashamed and guilty, lying awake and avoiding Tanvir in the corridors.

qa.q: What did Seema decide to do next time, and why is that a good use of guilt?
qa.a: To say stop or go to a teacher; it turns regret into a plan instead of more hiding.

qa.q: What might Seema's apology have meant to Tanvir?
qa.a: Tanvir seemed quietly relieved; since most people pretended they weren't there, being acknowledged made him feel less alone 🤍

grounding: Shows a young adult who regrets watching and doing nothing, then uses that shame to apologise and decide how to act next time.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
Monsoon rain hammered the railway footbridge at 6:15, and the 6:22 fast was Naveen's last chance to reach home before his daughter's school play.
Halfway across, a woman in a green saree sat down suddenly against the railing, then slid sideways, her bag spilling. People stepped around her, umbrellas tilted. Nobody stopped.
Naveen slowed. Maybe she's just tired, he thought. If it were serious, someone would be helping. A man glanced down at her, then glanced at the crowd, and kept walking. That glance caught Naveen: everyone was reading everyone else.
He turned back and knelt. "Madam? Can you hear me?" Her eyes fluttered. "Lakshmi," she whispered. "Dizzy."
Naveen called for an ambulance, then waved to a railway police constable at the stairs. The 6:22 thundered below. He stayed, holding his umbrella over her, until the stretcher came.

qa.q: Which train was Naveen trying to catch?
qa.a: The 6:22 fast.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when he first slowed down?
qa.a: Naveen felt unsure and hesitant, taking the calm crowd as proof it wasn't serious, and anxious about missing his train.

qa.q: What helped Naveen break out of the crowd's pattern?
qa.a: Noticing the man glance at the crowd instead of the woman showed him everyone was copying each other, so he checked for himself.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Lakshmi as people stepped around her?
qa.a: Lakshmi was probably frightened and helpless, dizzy on a wet bridge while umbrellas passed by.

grounding: Shows a commuter who sees a woman collapse while the crowd walks on, each person reading the others' calm as proof it is not serious.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
The badminton hall at the community centre went silent when Mr Joshi, a Sunday doubles regular, sat down heavily on court two and didn't get up. Twelve people stood frozen, rackets in hand. Someone said, "Should we call someone?" Nobody moved.
Sudha, who ran the front desk, walked straight onto the court and pointed.
"You, in the blue shirt. Call an ambulance now, give them the address on that board." Imran blinked, then dialled.
"You two, move the benches back so there's space."
"You," to a teenager by the net, "go to the front gate and wave the ambulance in."
"Anita, bring water and his bag."
Within a minute everyone had a job. Sudha knelt by Mr Joshi, talking to him quietly, until the paramedics came through the door the teenager held open.
Afterwards, Imran said, "I was standing right there. I just needed someone to point at me."

qa.q: How many people stood frozen on the court?
qa.a: Twelve people stood frozen.

qa.q: What does Imran's comment afterwards reveal about how Imran felt at first?
qa.a: Imran felt stuck and unsure, willing to help but frozen until someone pointed and gave a clear job.

qa.q: Why did Sudha's pointing work when "Should we call someone?" didn't?
qa.a: A question to everyone lets each person wait for another; naming one person for each task made the duty clear.

qa.q: What was it like for Mr Joshi once Sudha took charge?
qa.a: He likely felt less alone and frightened, with Sudha beside him and help clearly on its way.

grounding: Shows an adult breaking bystander freeze in an emergency by pointing at specific people and giving each a named task.

passage:
Monday: Ms Rao put Minakshi, Karthik, Sana and Joy together for the water-saving poster. Karthik drew a big tap. Sana wrote the slogan. Minakshi coloured one raindrop and played with her eraser. It's everyone's poster, she thought. Nobody will know who did what.
Wednesday: Karthik stayed in at break to finish the lettering. "Minakshi, can you do the border?" "Later," she said, and went out for hopscotch.
Friday: Ms Rao pinned the poster up. "Well done, group three!" Everyone clapped. Then she asked, "Who drew the tap? Who wrote the slogan?" Karthik and Sana put up their hands. "And the border?" Joy did. Minakshi looked at her one raindrop and felt her cheeks go warm.

qa.q: What did Karthik draw on the poster?
qa.a: Karthik drew a big tap.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi's cheeks go warm on Friday?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, because when Ms Rao asked who did each part, it was clear how little she had done.

qa.q: What could Ms Rao do at the start of the next project to stop one child coasting?
qa.a: Give each child a named part at the beginning, so everyone knows their job will be seen.

qa.q: What might Karthik have felt staying in at break while Minakshi played?
qa.a: Karthik was probably annoyed and tired, doing extra work while the praise went to the whole group.

grounding: Shows a child letting the rest of the group do the poster because shared credit makes doing less feel unnoticed.

passage:
In Class 5C at a Nagpur school, the last project ended with Pradeep drawing one cloud while Riya did the rest. So this time Hansa ma'am pinned a chart by the board: GROUP 2, SOLAR SYSTEM MODEL. Riya: planets. Pradeep: sun and labels. Mehul: stand. Asha: fact cards.
"Tick your box when your part is done," she said. "On Friday, each of you shows your own part."
Pradeep read his name twice.
On Wednesday he wrote a question mark after PLUTO, because he'd found out it isn't called a planet anymore. By Friday every box had a tick. When his turn came, Pradeep held up the sun and explained why it was so much bigger than the rest.
Riya whispered to Asha, "Finally, I didn't do it all."

qa.q: What was Pradeep's part in the model?
qa.a: Pradeep's part was the sun and labels.

qa.q: What does Pradeep reading his name twice suggest?
qa.a: Pradeep seemed surprised and a little proud to have a job with his name on it, which made the work feel like it mattered.

qa.q: Why did Hansa ma'am's chart work without any punishment?
qa.a: Each child could see their own job and knew they would show it on Friday, so effort was visible and nobody could hide.

qa.q: How is this project different for Riya?
qa.a: Riya feels relieved instead of overloaded, because this time the work is truly shared 😊

grounding: Shows a teacher giving each child a named part and showing who did what, so loafing shrinks without punishment.

passage:
The history project was due at 8 a.m., and at 9 p.m. the power went out across the colony.
In the group chat, Jagdish was typing by torchlight: "Doing the timeline on paper, will send a photo." Rhea: "Finishing sources on my phone." Tara had gone quiet.
Chandrika lay on her bed under the dead fan and sent a thumbs-up. Her one job had been the title page, done in ten minutes last week. She'd known from the start that Jagdish would never let the project fail. That was the clever part, she told herself.
When Rhea wrote, "Anyone free to check dates?", Chandrika's thumb hovered. Then she put the phone face down.
At 7:50 the next morning Jagdish handed in the folder, eyes red. Ma'am said, "Great work, all four of you." Chandrika smiled along, and felt something small and sour in her stomach. She didn't mention the title page.

qa.q: What time did the power go out?
qa.a: At 9 p.m., across the colony.

qa.q: What did Chandrika feel when Ma'am praised all four of them?
qa.a: Chandrika felt a mix of relief and guilt, "something small and sour" in her stomach, knowing she had only done the title page.

qa.q: What could Chandrika have done when Rhea asked for help?
qa.a: She could have offered to check the dates, a small job she could do by phone even without power.

qa.q: What was the night like for Jagdish?
qa.a: Jagdish was likely worn out and a little resentful, working by torchlight until the red-eyed morning while sharing credit equally.

grounding: Shows a teenager doing the minimum on a group project, relying on the diligent ones, feeling half clever and half guilty and not admitting it.

passage:
Lakshmi, you say your group leaves the whole science model to you? Sit. Let your Abhinav thatha tell you something.
Class 9, Madurai, long ago. Our teacher put four of us on a river-system chart: Ravi, Selvam, Mani and me. Within a week, I was the only one drawing. Ravi said his handwriting was bad. Selvam had cricket. Mani just smiled.
I didn't complain. I thought they'd call me bossy, the one who thinks he's the teacher. So I sat up by the kerosene lamp, grinding my teeth, and the anger sat in me like a stone. The night before submission, I tore a whole page because one line was crooked.
My amma saw and asked what was wrong, and I told her everything. Next morning I told Selvam plainly, "You colour the mountains, or your name comes off the chart."
He coloured them. Badly. But he did it.

qa.q: What reason did Ravi give for not drawing?
qa.a: Ravi said his handwriting was bad.

qa.q: How did young Abhinav feel while doing the chart alone?
qa.a: He felt angry and resentful, the anger sitting "like a stone", but afraid that complaining would make the others call him bossy.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Telling his amma and then speaking plainly to Selvam; saying it aloud let the anger out and made the work shared.

qa.q: How might Selvam have felt when Abhinav spoke so plainly?
qa.a: Selvam was probably surprised and a little embarrassed that the quiet one had noticed, which is why he did his part.

grounding: Shows a conscientious student doing most of a shared task alone, growing quietly resentful because complaining might look bossy.

passage:
With the design submission two days away and Mehul home with fever, the four of them were already short of hands. At 10 p.m. Binita looked around the studio: Ananya cutting foam board, Kiran fixing the model's roof, and Pankaj on the sofa, laptop open to the same slide he'd opened at six. "Almost done with the render," he said. He'd said that yesterday too.
Nobody answered. Pankaj had been their friend since first year; he'd sat with Kiran through a whole night at the hospital once. Calling him out felt like kicking someone who had helped you.
Binita watched Ananya slice the board harder than needed. Kiran didn't look up. At midnight Ananya muttered, "Some of us are doing a four-person job," to no one in particular. Pankaj laughed as if it were a joke. Kiran's jaw tightened. The model would get finished, Binita thought, but something in the group was starting to crack.

qa.q: Who was home with fever?
qa.a: Mehul was home with fever.

qa.q: How does Binita feel watching the silent studio?
qa.a: Binita feels uneasy and torn: Pankaj is a loyal old friend, but the unfairness is clearly straining the others.

qa.q: How could the group raise it without attacking the friendship?
qa.a: One of them, perhaps Binita, could talk to Pankaj privately, say what is missing and ask what is going on before resentment grows.

qa.q: What is the night like for Ananya?
qa.a: Ananya is frustrated and resentful, slicing the board hard and finally muttering about a four-person job.

grounding: Shows team members staying silent about a friend who is not pulling his weight, while the unfairness slowly erodes trust.

subtype: Feeling anonymous in a large team [Actor]
passage:
I'm Simran, and I'm a little embarrassed about how I behaved during fest prep.
There were forty of us on the logistics team. At the big Sunday meetings I stood at the back, nodded and left early. When the coordinator asked for someone to count chairs, I thought, thirty-nine other people can do it. My name wasn't on anything. Honestly, who would notice?
Then Francis split us into pairs and put up a sheet: "Simran and Leela, registration desk, Gate 2."
Suddenly it was mine. I made queue signs at midnight, printed a backup list and got there at seven. When a parent thanked us both by name, I felt ridiculously proud.
Same person, same fest. The only difference was that my part could be seen.

qa.q: How many people were on the logistics team?
qa.a: There were forty of us on the logistics team.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when a parent thanked the pair by name?
qa.a: Simran felt ridiculously proud, because the work was visibly Simran's own.

qa.q: What could a big team learn from Simran's story?
qa.a: Give each person a small, named task that others can see, so no one feels their effort disappears in the crowd.

qa.q: How might Francis see the change in Simran after the pairs sheet?
qa.a: Francis would likely notice Simran go from leaving early to arriving at seven, and feel pleased the pairs idea worked.

grounding: Shows a student whose effort drops in a large, anonymous team but rises once their part is named and visible.

I'm Aarti, Vinita's lab partner, so I saw most of this from the next bench.
Our five-person team had a stats project due, and Pradeep hadn't done a thing in two weeks. Tanvi wanted to email the professor straight away. "He's just lazy," she said.
Vinita said, "Give me one day."
After class she caught Pradeep by the water cooler, away from us. I couldn't hear much, only that her voice stayed low and his shoulders slowly dropped. Later she told us, "He doesn't understand the software at all. He was too embarrassed to say, so he's been avoiding it." She'd offered to show him for an hour on Saturday. "And if nothing's done by Tuesday, we go to the professor together."
On Saturday I saw them in the library, two laptops open. By Tuesday Pradeep had uploaded his section. Not brilliant, but his.

qa.q: How long had Pradeep done nothing on the project?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: What do Pradeep's slowly dropping shoulders suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: Pradeep likely felt embarrassed at first and then relieved, as the problem he had been hiding finally came out in private.

qa.q: Why was talking to Pradeep privately first a good move?
qa.a: It uncovered the real reason, confusion plus avoidance, and gave him a fair chance and a clear deadline before going to the professor.

qa.q: How might Tanvi see Vinita's choice to wait one day?
qa.a: Tanvi may have felt impatient, sure Pradeep was simply lazy, but the result shows Tanvi there was more to it.

grounding: Shows a team member speaking privately to a coasting teammate before escalating, finding a hidden reason mixed with avoidance.
